newsitem.title: USA: Inmate in NY death penalty dispute found hanged.
newsitem.headline: Inmate in NY death penalty dispute found hanged.

text.p: The man at the centre of a battle between top New York officials over whether he should face the death penalty on charges of killing a policeman apparently hanged himself in his cell early Thursday, authorities said.

Angel Diaz, 27, was discovered by a guard at the Rikers Island jail with a belt around his neck and medical staff could not revive him, prison spokesman John Mohan said. He said Diaz was not on a suicide watch and was therefore allowed to keep his belt and other personal items.

"He was found at 12:45 a.m. with one end of a belt tied around his neck and the other end tied to the bars of his cell in an area of the prison where high-profile inmates are held," Mohan said. "It's an apparent suicide, but the medical examiner's autopsy has yet to be made."
Other officials indicated foul play was not suspected.

Mohan later disclosed that an unfinished, five-page note handwritten by Diaz and newspaper clippings of reports on his controversial case were found in the cell. He said the note and clippings were part of a prison probe into the death.

Diaz's case sparked an emotional public debate over capital punishment, which was reinstated in New York by Republican Gov. George Pataki a year ago. Diaz was facing first-degree murder charges and possibly the death penalty for allegedly shooting police officer Kevin Gillespie to death on a Bronx street March 14 after a carjacking.

In an unusual step, Pataki dismissed Bronx District Attorney Robert Johnson as prosecutor of the case because of Johnson's reservations about applying the death penalty and appointed another death-penalty proponent, State Attorney General Dennis Vacco, to handle the case.

"He (Diaz) lived a violent life and he died the same way. I mourn the death of Kevin Gillespie, that's whose death I mourn," said Pataki, who was relatively unknown until he defeated long-time Democratic Gov. Mario Cuomo in 1994 on a pro-death penalty platform.

Diaz had been indicted and was awaiting trial at the time of his death and Vacco said charges of second degree murder and first degree attempted murder would proceed against two others involved in the March shootout.

"He has now denied the system an ability to arrive at a just result concerning his case," Vacco said. "He is the only one who is responsible, not only for Gillespie's death but for his own death as well."
The death penalty is not mandatory in first degree murder cases in New York and prosecutors have the option to seek life imprisonment with or without parole.

In the conflict between Pataki and Johnson, the prosecutor sued the governor for reinstatement in the case. On Thursday both Johnson and Vacco said they expected that legal battle to continue on principle to clarify the governor's powers.
